walkthroughs.h2: Calculating pH of a weak acid
walkthroughs.body_html:
Approximation: [H+]^2 / [HA] = Ka. So [H+] = sqrt(Ka × [HA]).

Equivalently: pH = 1/2 (pKa - log[HA]). Valid when [HA] >> [H+].

Smaller pKa -> stronger acid (more dissociation). HCl pKa ≈ -7 (very strong). Ethanoic acid pKa 4.76 (weak).

Carbonic acid pKa1 ≈ 6.4. Phenol pKa ≈ 10. Water pKw = 14 at 25 °C (note: pKa of water itself ≈ 15.74).

mcqs.q: How does a buffer maintain its pH when small amounts of acid are added?
options: A buffer prevents any H+ ions from being added to the solution at all.
A primary alcohol is oxidised to an alkene by losing water.
A buffer destroys added acid by changing it into water vapour.
The conjugate base in the buffer reacts with added H+ to remove it, keeping pH nearly constant.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
options: A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
Strong and concentrated mean the same thing for acids.
A strong acid fully dissociates in water; a concentrated acid has a high amount of acid per volume — these are independent properties.
A buffer destroys added acid by changing it into water vapour.

mcqs.q: What is the product of mild oxidation of a primary alcohol?
options: An aldehyde (which can be further oxidised to a carboxylic acid).
A primary alcohol is oxidised to an alkene by losing water.
A primary alcohol is oxidised directly to a ketone.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
